blocks.x: New Englanders grow up on unfussy seafood like lobster rolls the way other people grow up on tacos or barbecue—foods so embedded in the way of life of a particular place that you don’t realize how special they are until you start traveling. Now, when I’m away from home, I find that lobster rolls are seen as an expensive delicacy. Yes, lobster rolls are special; they exist in the city’s glitzier and fine-dining restaurants, and their prices have skyrocketed in more recent years. But they’re also just as common at fast food counters in the suburbs and fishmonger docks up and down the coast. And just like paying $6 a gallon for gas on a California road trip, or $43 for a martini at Bemelman’s Bar in Manhattan, having a lobster roll in Boston is a worthwhile investment every once in a while. It's simply what you do when you’re here.

That being said, not all lobster rolls are created equal—and many (sometimes controversial) variations exist. A purist will say that a proper one must—must!—be served on a split-top bun that’s been griddled until golden brown, while others make compelling arguments for fancy swaps like brioche rolls. Then there’s the lobster meat itself, served either as a simply dressed cold salad (Maine style) or warm and buttered (Connecticut style)—but that’s more of a personal preference.
The good news? There are many, many lobster rolls to experience in Boston, ranging from textbook classics to more chef-driven interpretations. Here's where to find the best.

Row 34

Chef Jeremy Sewall knows a thing or two about good fish, and his popular Row 34 restaurants (with locations in Fort Point and in Cambridge’s Kendall Square) are where you go for excellent beer, interesting wines, and a chef’s sensibility. Here, the lobster roll is surprisingly personal, with lobster sourced from chef Sewall’s cousin Mark, who captains a boat in York Harbor, Maine. There are two versions here: a warm buttered roll with steamed tail, claw and knuckle meat and tucked into a traditional split-top bun; and the other, the Ethel’s Creamy Lobster Roll, named for Sewall’s grandmother and folded together with celery, red onion, pickles, mayonnaise, crème fraîche, lemon, celery salt and black pepper. The cold, creamy one comes on a rosemary brioche bun that is griddled to order and is nothing short of heavenly.

blocks.x: James Hook & Co. is the alpha and omega of Boston lobster rolls; a platonic ideal of what a lobster roll should be. The family-run seafood business operating on the Boston waterfront for over 100 years is an adorable, unassuming shack on shiny, transformed Atlantic Avenue downtown—this is where any good lobster roll tour of the city should begin (or end). The company ships over 50,000 pounds of lobster daily, both online and to wholesale distributors nationwide, so they know a thing or two about quality. The rolls here come in two sizes and two styles, either chilled or warm with butter. While you’re here, don’t overlook the other seafood specialties; the double-stuffed scallop, clam chowder, and lobster mac and cheese make for a perfect shared side.
Saltie Girl serves up its rolls in a stylish Back Bay restaurant.
Mike Cotrone / @mikecotrone
Saltie Girl

If James Hook is the lobster roll in its natural habitat, Saltie Girl is its glamorous, city-slicker cousin. This stylish Back Bay restaurant slings some of the best seafood on Newbury Street, in an elegant yet playful dining room overlooking the boutiques of Newbury Street. Its classic New England-style lobster rolls arrive perfectly coiffed, alongside a charmingly branded bag of Saltie Girl potato chips (add some caviar from the raw bar if you like). But the real insider move here? Ask your server about the secret, off-menu version of the lobster roll: the meat comes fried, sprinkled with Korean chili flakes and sweet corn butter, resulting in something richer, spicier, and considerably more decadent than a traditional version. It’s a sterling reminder that, even in a historic city like Boston, we don’t have to take our classics so seriously.

blocks.x: This Back Bay lobster oll comes on a house-made brown butter bun.
The Banks Seafood and Steak

The Banks is a crowd-pleaser of a restaurant—a perfect location in Back Bay, a lively bar scene, and an elevated menu of New England classics. The lobster roll here is an example of a perfectly adventurous recipe where the chef has improved on the original with a few tweaks, but none so heretical that they feel like a major departure from tradition. It comes on a house-made brown-butter bun, sprinkled with sea salt and chives, and served with Old Bay potato chips. The hot lobster roll is a standout—it’s par-cooked, then warmed in a “lobster beurre monté,” a classic French technique that glazes the meat and also helps infuse more lobster flavor into it. The result is a roll that is deceptively simple, yes, bursting with flavor.

Courtesy Eventide Fenway
Eventide Fenway

Originally from Portland, Maine, Eventide brought its contemporary take on New England seafood to the Fenway neighborhood as a seafood counter in 2017 before evolving into a full-service restaurant in 2023. The experience here is decidedly more Boston than Maine—it’s a bustling, popular spot for pre-Fenway Park drinks and snacks, less of a cozy, James Beard-recognized eatery than its progenitor in Portland—but Eventide did one key invention with it for the Hub: its brown butter lobster rolls. They come on a fluffy, bao-style steamed bun, drenched (in a good way) with browned butter and flecked with sliced chives.

blocks.x: The Sail Loft's lobster roll comes with thick, crispy fries.
Courtesy The Sail Loft
The Sail Loft

Nestled on the fringes of the North End within steps of the Freedom Trail, Faneuil Hall and the restaurants of Hanover Street, this institution feels like it’s been here forever. The Boston Sail Loft’s lobster roll is classic, with chilled lobster salad lightly dressed with mayonnaise and piled generously into a toasted bun. The thick, crispy fries that accompany it are a departure from the canonical bag of chips, but they’re a nice touch. There are fancier lobster rolls in Boston—but with perfect execution, stiff drinks and waterfront views, what else would you need?
Red’s Best at Boston Public Market

A great, no-frills option for travelers who want to understand where their seafood actually comes from, this counter inside Boston Public Market is dedicated to small, independent New England fishermen. And that direct connection to the local fishing community is what makes this experience special. The market itself—just steps from the Freedom Trail—is an easy stop while sightseeing, especially if you’re in the Faneuil Hall, North End, or Beacon Hill areas. The lobster rolls fresh and unfussy. While there’s no waterfront view or white tablecloth, there is something very Boston about enjoying solid seafood in a bustling public market surrounded by Bostonians going about their everyday lives. Plus: Save room for a doughnut from Union Square Donuts, or a popover from The Popover Lady.
